title: How to Make Disciples When You Feel Unqualified
excerpt: The sense that you're not ready is not a reason to wait. It is, strangely, the very condition Jesus has always worked with.
body:
You feel unqualified. You don't know the Bible well enough. You can't answer the hard questions. Your own walk with God is uneven, your prayer life is thin, and you're aware of sins you haven't beaten. Who are you to disciple anyone? Surely that's for the people who have it together, the pastors, the seminary graduates, the ones who seem to have arrived.

I want to take that feeling seriously and then dismantle it, because it has kept more ordinary believers silent than any false doctrine ever has. The sense of being unqualified is not a sign that you should wait. It is, strangely, the exact condition Jesus has always preferred to work with.

## The people Jesus chose were not qualified

Look at who Jesus actually called. Fishermen. A tax collector working for the occupying empire. Men who, on the night he needed them most, fell asleep and then ran. After Pentecost, when Peter and John stood before the religious authorities, those authorities "perceived that they were uneducated, common men, and they were astonished" (Acts 4:13). The thing that astonished the experts was not the disciples' credentials. They had none. It was that "they had been with Jesus."

That is the whole qualification. Not expertise. Not a finished character. Having been with Jesus, and being willing to bring someone else into his company. If Jesus had waited for qualified people, he would have built his church on the Pharisees, the most biblically literate men of their day. He passed over them and chose the unschooled. That choice is good news for you.

## God's pattern is to use the inadequate

This runs through the whole Bible. Moses protested that he couldn't speak (Exodus 4:10). Gideon pointed out he was the least in the weakest family (Judges 6:15). Jeremiah said he was only a youth (Jeremiah 1:6). Every one of them named a real inadequacy, and every one of them was sent anyway, because the power was never supposed to come from them. "My grace is sufficient for you," God told Paul, "for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul's response was to boast in his weakness, because it was the doorway through which God's strength came.

If you wait until you feel adequate, you will wait forever, and you will also have missed the point. The point is that God gets the glory precisely because the vessel was obviously insufficient on its own. Your inadequacy isn't disqualifying. It's the setup.

## You only have to be one step ahead

Here is the practical liberation. You don't have to be an expert. You only have to be one step ahead of the person you're discipling, and even that's not always true. You learned to pray a little before they did. You've read a few books of the Bible they haven't. You've walked with God through a few storms they're just now entering. That's enough to start. A person who's been hiking for a year can guide a person on their first day, even though both are far from the summit.

And you will grow fastest by teaching. There's a reason for the saying that you don't really know something until you've had to explain it. Preparing to open a passage with others will drive you into the Word more deeply than years of passive listening ever did. The disciple-maker is discipled by the making.

## Let the people see your unfinished self

The fear of being unqualified often hides a more specific fear: that someone will see the real you, the one still struggling, and conclude you're a fraud. So you imagine you have to project a finished Christian life. But the finished version isn't only impossible, it's the wrong goal. People are not formed by watching someone who has arrived. They're formed by watching someone who keeps returning to Jesus after they fall.

Paul, who wrote half the New Testament, called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15), present tense, not past. The most honest thing you can offer the person you disciple is not your competence but your repentance, modeled in front of them. Show them how a real Christian fails and gets back up, and you've taught them the most important skill there is.

## "I don't know" is a complete answer

Much of the unqualified feeling comes from dreading the question you can't answer. So settle this now: "I don't know, let's find out together" is not a failure. It's discipleship. It models intellectual honesty, it sends you both into the Word and to wiser believers, and it frees you from the exhausting fraud of pretending to know everything. The leader who fakes certainty teaches the others to fake it too. The leader who admits the edge of his knowledge teaches them that honest faith can live with unanswered questions, which it must.

## The command came to you, too

Finally, remember who received the Great Commission. Not a class of professionals. Eleven ordinary men, some of whom, Matthew tells us, were still doubting even as Jesus commissioned them: "And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted" (Matthew 28:17). And it was to those worshiping doubters that he said, "Go therefore and make disciples." He didn't wait for their doubt to resolve. He sent them through it.

The command came to people exactly as unfinished as you are. It came with a promise attached: "And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age" (Matthew 28:20). You were never asked to do this on your strength. You were asked to go, and promised company.

## This week

Stop waiting to feel ready. Name one person you could begin with. Pick one short passage you do understand, you don't need to understand all of Scripture, just the next thing. Invite them to read it with you, and when they ask something you can't answer, practice saying, "I don't know, let's find out."

The unqualified feeling will not fully leave, and that's fine. It's not a wall. It's the doorway God has always used. Walk through it.
